name: Inuit and Arctic peoples
summary: The peoples of the North American Arctic and Greenland: the Paleo-Inuit (including the Dorset culture) from about 2500 BCE, and the Thule people, ancestors of today’s Inuit, who spread east from Alaska around 1000–1300 CE.

knownFor.label: Kayak and umiak
knownFor.note: Skin-covered boats for hunting and travel.

knownFor.label: Igloo
knownFor.note: Snow houses built for winter hunting trips.

knownFor.label: Toggling harpoon
knownFor.note: A harpoon head that turns sideways inside the animal so it cannot slip out.

location.value: Arctic coasts and islands from Alaska across northern Canada to Greenland.
location.source: Wikipedia: Inuit; Wikipedia: Thule people; Wikipedia: Dorset culture

terrain.value: Tundra, sea ice and rocky coasts.
terrain.source: Wikipedia: Inuit; Wikipedia: Thule people; Wikipedia: Dorset culture

climate.value: Very cold; long dark winters and short summers.
climate.source: Wikipedia: Inuit; Wikipedia: Thule people; Wikipedia: Dorset culture

resources.value: Seals, whales, walrus, caribou, fish, driftwood, soapstone.
resources.source: Wikipedia: Inuit; Wikipedia: Thule people; Wikipedia: Dorset culture

disasters.value: Changes in sea ice; the Little Ice Age shortened the open-water hunting season and reduced the number of whales.

population.value: Small; probably tens of thousands at most.
population.source: Wikipedia: Inuit; Wikipedia: Thule people; Wikipedia: Dorset culture

urbanisation.source: Wikipedia: Inuit; Wikipedia: Thule people; Wikipedia: Dorset culture

disease.value: Diseases brought by whalers and explorers caused mass deaths; in the western Arctic the population fell by close to 90% in the 19th century.

migration.value: The Thule people spread east from Alaska (where they had developed by 1000 CE), reached Greenland by the 13th century and replaced the Dorset people by about 1300.

economicBase.value: Hunting sea mammals and caribou; fishing.
economicBase.source: Wikipedia: Inuit; Wikipedia: Thule people; Wikipedia: Dorset culture

tradeRoutes.value: Native copper from the western Arctic and meteoric iron from north-west Greenland passed between communities; trade with Norse Greenlanders.

wealth.value: Wealth meant skill and food shared within the group.
wealth.source: Wikipedia: Inuit; Wikipedia: Thule people; Wikipedia: Dorset culture

moneyAndTax.source: Wikipedia: Inuit; Wikipedia: Thule people; Wikipedia: Dorset culture

inequality.value: Mostly equal; successful hunters had influence.
inequality.source: Wikipedia: Inuit; Wikipedia: Thule people; Wikipedia: Dorset culture

governmentType.value: No state; each household had a head, and elders had great influence.

keyRulers.source: Wikipedia: Inuit; Wikipedia: Thule people; Wikipedia: Dorset culture

succession.value: Leadership by experienced hunters and elders.
succession.source: Wikipedia: Inuit; Wikipedia: Thule people; Wikipedia: Dorset culture

institutions.value: Sharing within households, and shamans (angakkuq) as healers and spiritual guides.

stability.value: Groups moved with the seasons and animals.
stability.source: Wikipedia: Inuit; Wikipedia: Thule people; Wikipedia: Dorset culture

eliteConflict.value: Disputes were settled by song duels and community pressure.
eliteConflict.source: Wikipedia: Inuit; Wikipedia: Thule people; Wikipedia: Dorset culture

armyAndTech.value: Bows, harpoons, spears; bone and stone tools.

majorWars.value: Feuds with neighbouring Dene peoples, such as the Bloody Falls massacre (1771); Norse sagas record meetings with the people they called “skrælingar”.

territoryChange.value: Spread across the whole North American Arctic.
territoryChange.source: Wikipedia: Inuit; Wikipedia: Thule people; Wikipedia: Dorset culture

alliancesRivals.value: Rivals of Dene and Cree peoples to the south over land; traded with Norse Greenlanders.

inventions.value: Kayaks, umiaks, dog sleds, snow goggles and sewn skin clothing.

scienceEducation.value: Detailed knowledge of ice, weather and animals passed on orally.
scienceEducation.source: Wikipedia: Inuit; Wikipedia: Thule people; Wikipedia: Dorset culture

openness.value: Adopted metal tools from Norse and later European traders.
openness.source: Wikipedia: Inuit; Wikipedia: Thule people; Wikipedia: Dorset culture

communicationTransport.value: Dog sleds over sea ice, kayaks and larger umiaks on open water; inuksuk stone markers guided travellers.

religion.value: Spirits of animals and the sea (Sedna); shamans.

languageWriting.value: Inuit languages (Inuktitut, Kalaallisut and others); syllabic writing introduced in the 19th century.
languageWriting.source: Wikipedia: Inuit; Wikipedia: Thule people; Wikipedia: Dorset culture

artsArchitecture.value: Carving in ivory, bone and soapstone; Dorset miniature carvings and masks; throat singing.
artsArchitecture.source: Wikipedia: Inuit; Wikipedia: Dorset culture (checked 9 Nov 2026)

socialStructure.source: Wikipedia: Inuit; Wikipedia: Thule people; Wikipedia: Dorset culture

sharedIdentity.value: A shared Inuit identity across countries.
sharedIdentity.source: Wikipedia: Inuit; Wikipedia: Thule people; Wikipedia: Dorset culture

dailyLife.value: Igloos (snow houses) in winter in some areas, sod houses, and skin tents in summer; diets of seal, whale, fish and caribou; skin clothing.

neighbours.value: Norse Greenlanders, Dene, Cree, later Europeans.
neighbours.source: Wikipedia: Inuit; Wikipedia: Thule people; Wikipedia: Dorset culture

ideasReligions.value: Christianity spread through missions in Greenland (from 1721) and Canada.
ideasReligions.source: Wikipedia: Inuit; Wikipedia: Thule people; Wikipedia: Dorset culture

colonisation.value: Came under Danish, British/Canadian, American and Russian rule.
colonisation.source: Wikipedia: Inuit; Wikipedia: Thule people; Wikipedia: Dorset culture

riseSignals.value: Thule whaling technology allowed rapid expansion.
riseSignals.source: Wikipedia: Inuit; Wikipedia: Thule people; Wikipedia: Dorset culture

peakPeriod.source: Wikipedia: Inuit; Wikipedia: Thule people; Wikipedia: Dorset culture

declineSignals.value: The Dorset culture disappeared between about 1000 and 1500; the Thule had replaced them by about 1300.

outcome.value: Inuit live today in Greenland (about 51,000), Canada (about 70,500 in 2021; Nunavut was created in 1999), Alaska and a few places in Chukotka.

sources.value: Wikipedia: Inuit; Thule people; Dorset culture.
sources.source: Wikipedia: Inuit; Wikipedia: Thule people; Wikipedia: Dorset culture

overallCertainty.value: Mostly known from archaeology and oral history; dates are approximate.
overallCertainty.source: Wikipedia: Inuit; Wikipedia: Thule people; Wikipedia: Dorset culture
